item.title: The idiot's reductio
item.description:
Subtitle: if you truly believed that...

Every once in a while, I encounter what I call the idiot’s reductio: “If you truly believed X, you’d do Y. Since you don’t do Y, you must not actually believe X.”

A special case is when people say “I don’t believe in/feel/have X. But if you truly did believe in X, you’d do a crazy and absurd thing. Since you don’t do this crazy and absurd thing, I conclude you don’t believe in X, and also X isn’t real.”

Almost always incredibly childish and a complete failure of theory of mind. Some examples:

  • If you actually believed in the Christian Bible, you’d avoid wearing mixed fibers. Therefore you’re a fake Christian and you should either be an atheist or believe in my specific flavor of liberal Christianity with no controversial components.
  • God is the only reason for human morality. If not for Christianity, people would murder their neighbors all the time. Therefore your atheism is fake and the Christian God is real.
  • If you actually thought abortion was murder, you’d firebomb a Walmart, and hold funerals for miscarriages. You haven’t firebombed a Walmart. QED.
  • If you actually thought factory farming is evil, you’d firebomb a Walmart.
  • If you actually believed in climate change, you’d firebomb a Walmart.
  • If you actually believed in AI doom, you’d firebomb a Walmart.
  • If Al Gore really believed in climate change, he wouldn’t fly to climate change conferences and would, I dunno, swim or something.
  • If you really believed in open borders, you’d leave your front door unlocked and house migrants yourself.
  • Erika Kirk does speeches and sometimes laughs on camera in interviews. Therefore, she’s not actually sad about her husband dying. Also the death was faked.
  • “She called her alleged rapist the day after, therefore she wasn’t raped.”
  • “If you actually believed in Communism you wouldn’t be using an iPhone”
  • “If Ayn Rand was a real capitalist, she wouldn’t take welfare”
  • When Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic to warn the world about AI doom, he got a cacophony of comments about how if he’s actually worried he’d stay and try to make AI safer from the inside.
    • When Evan, head of misalignment science at Anthropic, said he’s extremely worried and that’s why he’s staying and trying to make it better, the peanut gallery immediately pivoted to saying his beliefs must be fake because otherwise he would’ve quit.
    • Quitting is evidence of fake beliefs, and so is staying. It seems like the masters of the idiot’s reductio are conveniently always impervious to evidence!
  • When Buck wrote an emotional post about near-term AI doom, he got a lot of comments from the peanut gallery about how he’s “crying” and working on AI safety research instead of working towards pausing AI. Implicit: therefore your beliefs are fake.
  • When I wrote my recent, measured post about near-term AI doom and pivoting to pausing AI, I immediately got dozens of aggro comments about how I should either spend my last year to convince randos of milquetoast positions on alignment, or chill out in San Diego or something. Implicit: therefore your beliefs are fake.

I’m sure you’ve encountered the same.

I used to think the core issue was a failure to appreciate human differences while modeling other people. Everybody approaches grief/fear/dread/betrayal/worries about humanity’s extinction in different ways. Perhaps people weren’t previously aware of this?

I used to think that, but I now think the explanation is too clean, and ironically overly charitable. After thinking about it some and observing more examples in the wild, I think the failure is even worse than that: most people making the idiot’s reductio don’t even have enough imagination to model *their own* minds. Or worse, they have that imagination but choose not to use it.

For example, if somebody says that God is the only reason that people don’t go around murdering their neighbors, I used to buy into the belief that those specific people have broken moral compasses and don’t understand how other people can have moral commitments without a divine arbitrator. But I thought about it just a tiny bit more, and realized that if those specific people de-converted, it seems unlikely they’d go around murdering people. So not only do they lack a plausible other-people-model, they also lack a coherent self-model.

Similarly, when people are like “if you really believed in AI doom, you’d commit mass violence,” I used to think the only people who’d say this are psychopaths who really want to firebomb a Walmart, have minimal concept of cause and effect, are just itching for an excuse, and also incapable of modeling other people’s saner reactions.

A perfectly fine, unbombed, Walmart. Photo by Zack Yeo on Unsplash

But I thought about it a little bit more, and realized that of course the same people are, in addition to having poor ability/willingness to model cause and effect and other people, also (thankfully) low-agency, nonviolent, incapable of doing real stuff, etc. They, too, will not firebomb a Walmart.

So the people who make the strange modus tollens move of “I don’t believe in/feel/have X. But if you truly did believe in X, you’d do this crazy and ridiculous and absurd thing. Since you don’t do this crazy and ridiculous and absurd thing, I conclude that not only is X false, but you also don’t believe it” sure seem off – my tentative conclusion is that they have either severely diminished reasoning faculties or severely diminished willingness to use reason, even more so than I previously thought.

I’m not sure what the best response is in those circumstances. Two good options that come to mind are:

  1. A short, high-minded response, aimed at onlookers. “I don’t think Y is the best solution to X. Here’s what I do instead.” Limit it to 1-3 sentences.
  2. (verbal equivalent of) Honest laughter at the idiot’s reductio for being as honestly idiotic as it actually is. “Wait, wait, you’re telling me that the best way for me to reduce abortions in America is firebombing a Walmart? What a wise and moral strategy! Why didn’t I think of that?”
    1. Bonus points if you can laugh with your interlocutor rather than at them (maintaining the polite social fiction that this is an honest slip-up on their end), though that isn’t strictly required.

But either way, you should mostly not waste your time. Don’t make the mistake of taking the idiot’s reductio, or the people who voice it, seriously. “The discourse” is not real life!

item.title: A lab employee's guide to raising concerns
item.description:
If you're an employee at a frontier lab, you are one of the most powerful people in the world. Not because of your nine-figure equity or the work you do—your lab probably won't live or die on your research: there are other researchers at the company, and if you don't refactor that eval harness, someone else will.

Rather, your power comes from being able to raise your voice and speak out. If you don't speak up, either internally or externally, I'm not sure anyone else will.

Your voice matters

People say "your voice matters" as a cliche where you're one of thousands of people becoming a data point in a senator's polling, and that group perhaps moves the needle, but that's not what I mean here. I mean, the Chinese government has a file on you. You are arguably more valuable than a nuclear weapon. Just you, by yourself, literally matter a whole bunch.

You don't have to email Congress or talk to journalists. You can, and they would jump at the chance to talk with you — the labs are opaque to the public yet keep saying things like "everyone on Earth could die".

If you email congresspeople, many of them will be earnestly interested in what you have to say.

Jacob Coxon blew up because the world was very interested in his message. If you speak out loudly, you could be in every major newspaper and go on primetime TV the next day.[1]

If instead of speaking out externally, you do an internal push, I bet that you could, by yourself, cause the company to make drastically different decisions.

Figure out what to push for

A few asks you could try and push for include:

  1. Putting forward a concrete pacing plan and lobbying to mandate that pacing plan across companies.
  2. Greater transparency, such as robust incident disclosures or embedded auditing.
  3. Taking little things your company has done wrong recently and pushing for a fix.
    1. At OpenAI, push for a commitment to never look at employees' personal devices.
    2. At GDM, you could have pushed them to stop making employees sign an agreement to never speak ill of the company for the rest of their lives.
    3. At Anthropic, you could push for them to disclose their misalignment/rogue incidents at least as well as OpenAI has.

Being a lab employee gives you a unique viewpoint and voice

As a lab employee, you:

  1. Know things the public doesn’t about the rate of AI progress, what incidents have occurred, and whether your company is adhering to best safety practices.
  2. Have a platform to speak inside your company and to push your company to do things— both because the company has a culture of listening to its employees (it has to, to attract top talent), and because employees listen to each other.
  3. Are legibly credible to people outside the SF tech bubble. The public, Congress, and the defense community alike don't have an easy way to evaluate AI expertise: it's hard to tell who's a quack and who's not. Having actually worked at one of these companies is an instantly legible sign that someone knows what they're talking about. As such, there's a ton of demand to speak to company employees.

This is an incredible position, yet one that very few people leverage. Most people at AI companies, for whatever reason, seem either too afraid or too unsure of themselves to speak up.

I beg of you, get advice

It's hard to write a post like this. Quitting and agitating internally are spicy topics. Moreover, a lot of what makes sense to do is going to depend on the specifics of your situation and what you're comfortable with or feel you would be good at.

It is very difficult to make these choices when thinking in isolation, and it's very difficult to navigate this situation if you've never seen a situation like it before. I recommend working with someone who has supported concerned employees in the past with success. I especially recommend Jennifer Gibson of Psst, but I also think Lawrence Lessig or The Signals Network are great alternatives.

All of these groups are attorneys, so conversations are privileged and confidential. That means it's illegal to reprimand you for talking to them, and you can share NDAed information with them if it's in the course of getting legal advice: you're no longer thinking in a vacuum!

Moreover, all those groups work pro bono, so you don't have to pay them. You can reach out to them directly (Psst via Signal @PsstLegal.01, Lessig via lawlessig@proton.me and TSN via Signal @thesignalsnetwork.01). I recommend reaching out on a personal device. Have a low bar for reaching out. These folks would love to hear from people earlier rather than later. In fact, if you are reading this guide, consider just reaching out to them right now!

If it makes you more comfortable, you could also try reaching out to two to three friends you trust immensely who do not work at your company and talking to them (without revealing anything confidential). Or you can DM me here on LessWrong and I will help. Getting any advice is better than no advice.

Advisors will help you:

  1. Navigate any legal risks.
  2. Navigate comms if you want to talk to media. They can help you get better media or triage media that you're getting, and they can train you on how to respond to media.
  3. Reach out to important individuals to speak to, like members of Congress. (While the folks I've recommended talking to will have warm connections and be able to get you better meetings, you can also always just cold email staffers for members of Congress yourself. They will probably respond! They are very keen to talk to concerned AI company employees, but I think many people don't feel an affordance or enough comfort doing this, and so someone can help you navigate those conversations.)
  4. They might be able to help you speak out in legally protected ways.
  5. At a high level, they can help you brainstorm options and look out for gotchas. Of course, they won't have all the context you have, and all these advisors will want to amplify your strategic vision, but there's also a good chance they're tracking considerations you might have missed.

Consider being a tad cynical when planning

I think many company employees have a lot of faith and trust in their company. It's not my place here to argue about whether that trust is correct, but I would at least urge folks, when planning, to make plans that would not totally fall apart or backfire if more cynical assumptions about how these companies work hold true.

  • Do not communicate about your plans for quitting on work devices.
  • If possible, go out of your way to make it abundantly legible that you are a good, reliable, scrupulous employee who is beyond reproach. Do not give your employer excuses to discredit you. However, do not be deterred if you feel like you are not a great employee. I think many people get scared out of speaking up because they think that their company or peers will discredit them. In my experience, this rarely happens. Even if you are about to get fired, I think it can still be valuable to speak up.
  • If you want to speak out about something that's not sensitive, and you want to run it by the comms team, I strongly recommend framing it as giving them a heads up, not asking for permission. Give them a deadline by which to comment. I have never seen a comms team at a lab approve anything shaped like an employee speaking out on risk. Things just get added to the pile and never resolved.

There's more to life than your current job

I find that employees at AI companies are often shockingly worried about losing their job. If you work at an AI company, you are an extremely hot commodity. Many people would love to hire you. I have seen many people in this kind of position worry they will not get a job. All of them have immediately been showered with job offers. Many companies will literally try to look for when lab employees leave and then immediately try to snag them.

If you've spoken up and shown bravery and courage, this may make some very profit-driven large corporations more hesitant to hire you, but it will also give you an air of credibility in a space where legible, credible integrity is hard to come by. I think it will, on net, improve your career capital.

Choose whether or not to speak up internally

If you're considering quitting with a bang, you could first try to raise a bunch of concerns internally in Slack and perhaps complain loudly enough that the company fires you. You could also threaten to quit if the issue is not resolved.

If you want to stay at the company, you can also try to continuously raise concerns. Try to get a group of people together and push for whatever ask you picked above. Expand the group of people, keep pushing, and keep talking to people.

Note: Speaking up internally is often appealing because maintaining a collaborative culture within the company has genuine value and it's better if companies have a culture of doing the right thing. But it does have downsides. If you speak up internally, it can make it more difficult to decide to speak up externally without being identified. (If you're the person most clearly advocating for policy change X, then if it ever comes out that people outside the company are also calling for X, you will be a suspect.) People are dispositionally biased towards the easier option, and usually have too much faith in their company to change.

Choose whether or not to whistleblow

Whistleblowing means raising concerns that your company is doing something clearly reckless, unethical, or illegal, where either the world or specific policymakers are not aware and need to be.

The main way to whistleblow is by raising a concern to a specific individual. Depending on the circumstances, this could be Congress, the EU AI Office, the California Attorney General, the Securities and Exchange Commission, or another government agency. You have a lot of legal protections when talking to these folks. Whistleblowing is a legally protected right, and SB 53 creates some extra legal protections for whistleblowing about AI concerns in particular.

To get these legal protections, you have to go about things the right way. Do not try to figure this out yourself. For the love of all that is holy, talk to a whistleblowing lawyer.

You can also talk to journalists. If you talk to a journalist, make it clear to them that you are talking on background or off the record. If they agree to that, they will not name you. They are very protective of their sources. If you are talking to a journalist, make sure you are sharing concerns about how your company is behaving, especially dangerously, and where there is a clear public need to know. Confidentiality is important and should not be breached lightly.

The AI Whistleblower Initiative has written a guide to whistleblowing here.

Again: If you're even vaguely considering this option, please make sure you are getting legal advice!

Choose whether or not to speak up externally

Be the next Jacob Coxon!

  • You can either complain about specific practices at your company, or you can sound the alarm about AI risk more broadly. This doesn't necessarily mean critiquing your company. If you think that your company is "the good guy," you can still say you think risk is unacceptably high.
  • You can write a tweet thread. Your tweet thread should be easy to understand and digest. I beg of you, keep it concise and to the point, and do not bury the lede in euphemistic language that requires reading between the lines.
  • You can talk to journalists or go on TV.
  • You can write an op-ed.

If you're thinking to yourself, "I have no idea how I would place an op-ed or go on TV or talk to a journalist," I will refer you to the section on getting advice! Those advisors know how to do it, and it's easy peasy for them.

If you'll be doing media or writing an op-ed, I recommend giving the comms review folks at your company a heads-up, but not asking for their permission (because they will say no or will delay/block it).

Consider the optics of your actions

If you raise a public fuss, you might end up with a lot of eyes on you, and your actions will reflect on AI safety as a whole.

People might read into the place you work after you quit. If you leave OpenAI complaining about safety and then go to Anthropic, that will send a very specific message, which you should think through whether you endorse. If you start talking about AI safety and then also mix in a bunch of niche political views, people might associate those views with AI safety as a whole. If you get into a fight with Elon Musk on Twitter, maybe Elon will start hating all of AI safety...

That said, these considerations should not paralyze you or hold you back from raising a fuss: inaction is generally going to be much worse for AI safety than suboptimal action!

Tips and tricks

  • Remember that if/when you leave, you will lose access to most information. Therefore, if someone makes a claim like, "One time you said ABC," it will be very hard for you to refute. If you want to make claims like, "I have never said ABC," it'll be hard for you to be confident because you will not be able to check what you wrote as an employee.
  • If you are considering whistleblowing about a particular document and want to stay anonymous, opening that document many times, having a suspicious access pattern, or screenshotting that document on a work device will probably all be monitored by IT and may identify you.

But whatever you do, do something

You have the power here. You could unionize, you could whistleblow, you could agitate for a concrete pacing plan. You could write some strongly-worded complaints on Slack. But, do something.

You have the power here, but the window is closing. Every model you ship needs you a little less than the last one. It's unclear whether, in a post-AGI world, the labs will continue to exist.

Do good work while you’re in there.

  1. ^

    Though I think you should expect a somewhat smaller splash than Jacob made, just because he did get a bit lucky.

item.title: Epoch's newly Bayesian ECI is sensitive to how 100% scores are clipped
We can still win against ASI (maybe)
item.description:
This essay is a combination of personal notes, discussions I had at the MAIA/AIST workshop, and slides from a talk I gave with JHU ASBS and BlueDot Impact.

Premise

A common theme I noticed, particularly among viewpoints with short timelines, is the idea that the introduction of ASI is inherently and instantaneously the loss condition. This stems, I think, from Yudkowsky-ian philosophy that ASI = unavoidable doom.[1] I think this defeatist attitude is counterproductive and detracts from real, important, effective avenues of action.

A superintelligence is bounded through interaction with the physical world; there are fundamental limitations on feedback loops which are crucial to enact any kind of influence.[2] ASI on a laptop in a concrete room in 1850 cannot escape with any high probability, and even if it did, it would take a very long time for it to do anything – conceivably much longer than the physical lifetime of the laptop. In well-defined worlds like video games, it is not hard to imagine scenarios where you are mathematically guaranteed to lose even with perfect skill and play – for example, if the ball in pong is much much faster than your paddle. There is an analogy here to galactic algorithms in computer science[3]: just because an ASI has an algorithm that scales better asymptotically doesn't mean the constant factors (e.g. time needed to conduct experiments; time needed to manufacture a quantity of robots) allow it to win within a finite time horizon.

In the present world, incidents like HuggingFace[4] can be largely attributed to 1. Ease: cybersecurity and the internet is an extremely accessible attack surface for AI, 2. Lack of foresight: most of the internet was not designed in anticipation of highly intelligent adversaries and widespread integration into society (cybersecurity is almost always reactionary), and 3. Ubiquity: the internet is a widespread and well-connected infrastructure tied deeply to society. As I, and many others have previously wrote, it is extremely difficult for ASI, if incarnated right now, to rapidly destroy all of humanity, or even do more mundane things like synthesize a virus or take over a factory. It would almost necessarily have to use humans, through superpersuasion or blackmail, limiting the effective set of “hands” to a few experts which it must coordinate… not impossible, but inherently gated by the limitations of humans as tools: we suck at following instructions, general competency, etc. Physical limits also significantly bound the influence of ASI in propagation time and physical limits (e.g. Control Theory); no matter what, noise and experiment mean you cannot have iteration speeds past a certain limit nor achieve results under a certain statistical confidence. All of this is further compounded by the need to avoid detection prior to achieving independence or dominance over humanity. This is why “gradual disempowerment” scenarios are generally more favored.[5]

However, as I have previously argued, this will change.[6] It’s only through luck that the robotics and biotech industries have not achieved the same widespread diffusion that the internet has (at this point in time), and all signs point towards this changing rapidly. This presents us a simple theory of change: designing these new systems with foresight, similarly to how we treat other high-risk technologies like nuclear weapons. Through proactively “hardening” these systems – these “hands” for AI – can we provide an effectively externally-imposed slowdown (allowing other actions) or even shut down ASI?

Adjusting time-to-doom through slowing the trajectory of ASI independence

We have three basic actions to combat against ASI: slow it, see it, stop it. Suppose a misaligned ASI has escaped: we define the win condition as a physical base (power, chips, robots, etc.) entirely independent of humanity. Here, we have four steps:

  1. Building/accumulating physical assets takes some amount of time.
  2. Each month, there is some chance someone notices.
  3. Each time someone notices, some action may be taken for a response.
  4. A response either terminates the ASI, or sets it back.[7]

item.title: Tracing Feature Circuits
item.description:
Neuronal superposition is the phenomena where a neuron in a model activates on many unrelated concepts. This is a problem for interpretability research because you don't have a 1:1 mapping of a neuron and a clean, human-interpretable feature. Sparse dictionary learning offers a potential solution to this problem whereby a neuron in a model is mapped, through an autoencoder, to each of the features it activates. It offers a method to distill the many features embedded in a single neuron to a single feature activation.

Now imagine you could decompose each component of a model (the MLP layers and attentional units) into a sparse dictionary of features such that for a single input prompt, you have a mapping of which native model components correspond to which sparse dictionary features. The dream scenario is each of the autoencoders' features are monosemantic, interpretable, and you could replace each component (i.e. layer 5 attention head 6) with these features; thereby decomposing a black box into interpretable autoencoder parts.

The goal of this research direction to start with a behaviour in GPT-2, replace GPT-2 with transcoders (an autoencoder variant), and find the relevant features that produce this behaviour. In other words, identifying feature circuits that decompose a model into interpretable subparts that together define some behaviour in GPT-2.

What is being replaced?

The method to find a feature circuit starts with replacing each attentional unit and MLP component at every layer in GPT-2 with a transcoder. Usually a transcoder is applied to the MLP of a model and learns to reproduce the activations post MLP from the pre MLP activations. However, because the attention mechanism mixes information across token positions, a different transcoder architecture is needed. I use 3 transcoder architectures to fully replace GPT-2, 1 to replace the query-key circuit, 1 to replace the value circuit, and 1 to replace the MLP components.

1. Query and key features

The query-key transcoder follows my earlier post. They are two separate transcoders; the query transcoder learns a sparse set of features for every token and the key transcoder does the same. In practice L0 (the number of features active per token) ranges from about 10-20 features. Generally, earlier layer transcoders have L0 on the small side of this range and later layers require more features to reconstruct the attention pattern.

The activation of a feature for either the query or key transcoder is given by:

aBt,f = max(0, xt · eBf + cBf).

where eBf is the encoder or the transcoder's read direction. The decoder or write direction determines how much a feature contributes to the output. For a single attention head h, the reconstructed query and key are

q̂t,h = bQh + Σi aQt,i uQi,h,   k̂s,h = bKh + Σj aKs,j uKj,h.

and the transcoder's efficacy determines how well the final attention pattern is reproduced by one head:

Ŝh,t,s = q̂t,h · k̂s,h / 8

So, the query-key transcoder takes normalized residual stream activations as the input and learns to reconstruct every attention head's attention pattern using learned features from separate query and key transcoders. These transcoders are trained on every layer of GPT-2 to replace the QK part of the attention computation throughout the model.

2. Multi-token value features

Next I trained a 8192 value MTC (multi token transcoder) on each layer of GPT-2. The transcoder learns what information should be moved from source token positions to destination token positions. It reads the same normalized residual stream activations as the query-key transcoder and produces sparse activations, aVs,f for every residual stream vector. Its decoder has one 64-vector per feature per head, plus a per-head bias. This gives v̂s,h = bVh + Σf aVs,f uVf,h. During training I route these decoded values with the teacher’s frozen attention pattern so a source feature is transported to its destination token as per the model's native attention pattern routing.

ẑt,h = Σs≤t A*h,t,s v̂s,h

Lrecon = λ · mean[(flatten(ẑ) − flatten(z*))²].

The transcoder's output reconstruction is z hat and has shape [T, 12, 64]. It reproduces each of the 12 attention heads' 64-dimensional activation. The loss measures how well it reproduces the flattened z activation in GPT-2 which has shape, [T, 768] (where 12*64 = 768). A MTC feature that activates on a source token can contribute to each of the 12 heads for a particular destination token, and the contribution is determined by the transcoders' decoder or write direction.

3. MLP features

For each MLP I use the publicly released GPT-2 small transcoders from Dunefsky, Chlenski and Nanda. Each has 24,576 features. It reads the standardized post-attention residual y (before the second LayerNorm’s learned gain and bias), and predicts the native MLP output at the same position:

aMt = ReLU(ytEM + cM),   m̂t = bM + Σf aMt,f uMf.

Now we have a means to replace each uninterpretable component (MLP and attentional units) in GPT-2 with monosemantic, interpretable features at every layer in the model. To identify a subset of features that are salient to a model's output for a given prompt, we need some way to trace how a model uses the replaced transcoder features to compute its output.

Attribution Graphs

An attribution graph is a tool used to visualize and map the internal steps a model takes when turning a specific prompt into output logits. They break down opaque black box LLM behaviour into a set of active features as they pertain to the input tokens and output logits. Edges between nodes are defined by the Jacobian a · ∂Jb/∂a. For some edge between A --> B, A writes something that B reads and the edge is determined by how much that write pushes B's objective up or down on a given prompt. Here a is the feature’s activation. Starting from a target node (such as a specific token logit or an active feature), the computation traces backward using the Jacobian matrix to measure how earlier nodes influence later ones.

If I simply stack 12 sets of imperfect predictions, an early error changes what every later encoder sees and errors accumulate. This is why nodes are input tokens, output logits, features and error nodes. The error nodes for the query-key transcoder, MTC, and MLP transcoders respectively are given by:

εS = S* − Ŝ on allowed source–destination pairs;
εz = z* − A* v̂ at each destination and head;
εM = m* − m̂ at each token.

That is the sense in which this is a complete replacement model: learned branches cover both sublayers of every block, with explicit accounts for what they miss. Token and position embeddings, residual connections, normalization, output projections and unembedding remain part of the scaffold. Thus during a forward pass, error nodes keep the native GPT-2 logit predictions faithful to the replaced forward pass with transcoder features. Additionally, rather than freezing the attention pattern, the attention computation is kept dynamic and can change inside the attribution graph. This way, query and key features can be traced directly from slight changes in the attention pattern and I can identify whether a change in attention routing matters for a particular output logit.

Note that attribution graphs to find circuits of features exists and was popularized by Anthropic - Tracing Attention Computation Through Feature Interactions. However, an attribution graph for a single prompt can highlight many features, some of which may not be especially relevant to the model's computation. What I introduce is a method that curates a small subset of features that matter most for a particular model behaviour.

For instance, after “The box is too heavy”, why does GPT-2 prefer to continue with to rather than that? A graph of this one prompt might turn up features specific to heavy or box, but are irrelevant to the grammatical nuance that predicts to rather than that. What I want to find is the part of the computation that also matters after “The room is too small” and “The path is too narrow”.

From one prediction to a family of feature graphs

For each of the aforementioned 3 prompts, I start with a separate attribution graph for each of the 3 prompts and define D = logit(“ to”) − logit(“ that”) for all 3. Thereby identifying the part of the model computation I'm interested in. A positive D means the model prefers to over that.

First, give the prompts a common set of candidates. Within each prompt, I nominate active query, key, value and MLP features based on edges in the attribution graph. Then I find the features that activate across multiple prompts, denoting them as potential features that are integral to the 'to' - 'that' mechanism. I match a feature by its layer, its kind (query, key, value, or MLP), and its ID. I count how many distinct prompts retain the feature after pruning the attribution graph.

For example, layer 8 key feature 888 and layer 8 value feature 7733 each had a surviving attribution edge into layer 8 head 4 in all three prompts. That gives me a specific question to test: does removing the key feature’s contribution to that head change the preference for the output logit? What about removing the value feature’s contribution? In all, the shared graphs yielded 50 feature interventions to try. The native GPT-2 ablation in the next section retained 16 at τ = 0.05. Those are two different findings: the graphs tell me which features repeatedly appear on influential paths; the ablations tell me which removals actually move the prediction by the amount I specified.

τ ablation: which proposed features matter in native GPT-2?

Identifying candidate features across multiple prompts reduces the number of features that are relevant to a particular output logit direction for a family of prompts, but it doesn't answer how relevant the feature is. We need some way to measure how salient a feature is to the native GPT-2 internal computation. This is where the feature ablations enter the methodology.

What gets ablated? On “The box is too heavy”, the value transcoder assigns V7733 an activation of 7.23 at the word too in the clean run. Its decoder gives me a 64-dimensional vector u for head 4. When native GPT-2 computes that head’s value vector v at too, I replace it with v − 7.23u. I’ve subtracted precisely the write that the transcoder assigned to this feature at this position and head.

The same operation applies to the other branches. For a query I subtract the feature’s write from the native query at the destination; for a key or value I subtract it at the source, where it can affect any destination that reads it. If a feature has surviving connections to several heads at a position, I test those head slices together. An MLP feature has no head index: I subtract its 768-dimensional write from the native MLP output at its active positions.

What earns a feature a place in the subset?

I start with an empty set S, and features are iteratively added to the set if ablating the feature from the GPT-2 forward pass decreases the logit difference (D = logit(positive token) − logit(negative token)) by some amount greater than τ. Specifically I compare a forward pass on GPT-2 with the set S of features removed, and another forward pass with set S plus feature f removed. The difference is the extra drop caused by this particular feature's removal:

δp(f | S) = Dp(S) − Dp(S ∪ {f}).

I average the ablation effect across all prompts in the family of prompts and retain a feature in the subset if the average drop is greater than τ. Feature retention means every subsequent ablation trial includes this feature in the mass removal. If a feature's average drop is not greater than τ, I leave it out and test the next candidate feature against the same set as before.

This process defines a salient subset of features for a particular model behaviour. If the model's behaviour of interest is defined by the logit difference, then subtracting a feature's decoder write direction from the model's native activation must make a measurable additional difference to the family of prompt's prediction. Figure 1 shows the subset this search found for the family of prompts "The box is too heavy", "The room is too small", "The path is too narrow", for D = logit(“ to”) − logit(“ that”).

Figure 1. The retained graph at τ = 0.05 for “The box is too heavy,” “The room is too small” and “The path is too narrow.” Read from earlier layers at the bottom. The 3/3 badges count discovery prompts. Q - query feature, K - key feature, V - value feature and M - MLP feature.

Model steering using the feature subset

Once a subset of features has been identified, one way of testing if this array of features is actually relevant to the model's internal computation is by steering the model. We can steer the model in the direction of these features to bring out a behaviour on a prompt that lacks the behaviour of interest. For instance, GPT-2 reads "The task is so difficult" and predicts that. Can I make it predict to by leveraging the set of features retained on the family of prompts “The box is too heavy,” “The room is too small” and “The path is too narrow".

I run two forward passes, the first being the donor on the too prompt and retain the activations for the subset of features. The second pass runs the so prompt or the recipient. During this second pass I replace selected features' current contribution with the donor activation: (donor activation − current recipient activation) × decoder vector.

By transplanting the 16 retained features, the to-that logit difference moved from −1.183 to +0.740 and the top prediction changed from that to to. Model steering shows that for a potential feature circuit, the same features acting jointly transfers that preference to a new prompt.

Case Studies

Neither / either contrast pair

I found a seven-feature set on the nor − or contrast at τ = 0.40. It contained L0 MLP6426 and MLP14402, L1 MLP6988, L2 MLP22278, and three layer-9 features connected to head 10: K626, V1402 and V7171. Subtracting these feature directions swapped logit direction on all 3 prompts: “They wanted neither bread,” “She chose neither wine,” and “He bought neither rice.” By removing these features from the GPT-2 forward pass, all 3 prompts predict 'or' instead of 'nor'. Similarly, either-donor steering into a neither-recipient reversed 4/4 matched pairs. For “We preferred neither salmon,” the matched either donor moved D from +3.373 to −0.741 and the overall next-token prediction from nor to or.

The two layer-0 MLP features made it possible to ask a cleaner question. I locked just those two IDs, matched the actual token neither, and compared each removal alone and both together on three new prompts. Here is the bread example:

At the token “neither”

D = nor − or

Top next token

Native GPT-2

+3.101

nor

Remove L0 MLP6426

+2.483

nor

Remove L0 MLP14402

+2.786

nor

Remove both

−1.209

and

This demonstrates that features can act jointly, where multiple features glean distinct information relevant to some underlying mechanism. By removing only one feature, the underlying mechanism can remain mostly intact, but joint removal completely erases the model's ability to reproduce said mechanism.

Figure 2. Each bar is a native GPT-2 forward pass. The joint removal crossed zero on bread, wine and rice.

Either / both: a candidate route from cue to final noun

Here D = or − and. In “She wanted either tea,” L8 V7783 writes at either, and L8 Q1314 writes at the final noun, tea, in head 5. Layer 9 contains another such arrangement: V1633 at the cue and Q938 at the final noun in head 10. L9 MLP12401 and L10 MLP171 and MLP3189 write at the final noun. This gives the graph a concrete interpretation: information available at the cue can be routed to the position where the continuation is predicted. The measurements below test the whole group; they don’t isolate either individual head as the required route.

Figure 3. Four edges from the retained “or − and” subgraph for “She wanted either tea” at τ = 0.15. Read each arrow from a feature firing to a head at its destination.

The 11-feature set at τ = 0.15 reversed 3/3 discovery prompts (reversal means logit difference went from positive to negative). When I transferred the ablation scope, L10 That eleven-feature intervention reversed 5/5 evaluated prompts, including two new ones, and made and top-ranked on all five.

With the twelve-feature steering group, either donors reversed 3/4 both recipients; both donors reversed 2/4 either recipients. One pair worked both ways. “She wanted both tea” went from −7.108 to +0.685 with the either donor, changing the top word from and to or. The reciprocal transplant into “She wanted either tea” moved +3.715 to −0.463, changing or back to and.

Too / so: the most consistent steering result

“The task is too difficult” invites to (“to finish”). “The task is so difficult” invites that (“that nobody finished”). I kept D = to − that fixed. The group at τ = 0.05 had 16 feature identities: ten MLP, one query, four key and one value. On a representative prompt, L0 MLP20928 fired at too, L1 Q2179 wrote into head 3 at the final adjective, and L8 K888 and V7733 both wrote into head 4 at the cue.

Subtracting all sixteen features flipped only 1/3 discovery prompts. “The room is too small” went from +5.234 to −1.895, but the box and path prompts stayed positive. Steering gave a different result: too donor → so recipient reversed 5/5 pairs, including both held-out lexical variants.

Figure 4. The same sixteen feature identities transferred in both directions. Open circles mark the native recipient margin and diamonds mark the result after replacement. The asterisks mark prompts held out of feature selection.

Discussion

The question I started with was how a word near the beginning of a prompt can change a prediction several tokens later. After “She wanted either tea”, for example, what carries information about either to the point where GPT-2 favors or? I want a feature subgraph that explains those steps. In this case the graph points to a specific route worth testing. Layer 8 value feature 7783 fires at either, and head 5 reads from that position at tea, where the model makes its prediction.

To find a subgraph like this, I choose two possible next tokens and build a separate attribution graph for their logit difference on each prompt in a family. I keep features and connections that recur as the wording changes. Then I test each proposed feature in native GPT-2 by subtracting its decoded contribution at the token positions and heads identified by the graph. The positive τ sweep keeps the removal when it lowers the family’s average margin by more than τ. This gives me a candidate feature circuit that plausibly explains a GPT-2 behaviour as it pertains to a specified logit difference.

The primary limitation of this approach is the absence of proof of a comprehensive circuit. The ablation and model steering tests highlight that a given subset of features are important for computing a particular model mechanism, but they don't prove that a circuit of features are minimal, sufficient, or complete. The main area of future work would revolve around conducting tests that demonstrate minimality, sufficiency, and completeness for a proposed feature circuit.

item.title: Making sense of Recursive Self Improvement
item.description:
This is a linkpost from my newsletter: https://invertedpassion.substack.com/p/making-sense-of-recursive-self-improvement

There’s a whiff of an imminent RSI in the air. The theoretical possibility of AIs recursively improving themselves autonomously until we hit singularity has always existed but the recent METR report seems to have spooked a lot of rationalists and AI insiders about how soon it can arrive.

The report that triggered the fear and paranoia is this one, and the chart to pay attention to is the following:

It effectively shows how the rate of progress in AI R&D has roughly doubled at Anthropic since October 2025, and METR attributes most of the acceleration to Anthropic’s own use of AI in R&D. Before moving on to making sense of what’s driving this and its potential implications, keep two caveats in mind:

  1. This report redacted many important datapoints as Anthropic didn’t let METR share them
  2. Anthropic is soon going public, so it is in their best interest to project an acceleration (Keep this in mind for the other Anthropic charts below too: they’re from their IPO roadshows)

Despite these caveats, I will make the case that a crude form of recursive improvement in AI models is already happening and it’s simply going to become more sophisticated and significantly scaled up. And whatever we call ASI at the end of it is likely to be jagged.

Current self-improvement: AI models accelerating AI models releases

Well, models are releasing faster lately. There are several factors driving it and perhaps the biggest one is the sprawling data-generation industry that’s $10bn now, growing rapidly and perhaps could be $100bn in a few years. These data generation companies make RL environments to sell to labs on as many economically useful tasks as they can codify.

What does a typical RL environment look like? Imagine slicing the entire economy into sectors and then sub-sectors and sub-sub-sub sectors, and then hiring an expert to design context, task and success rubrics for each one of them. As an example, imagine Finance → Private Equity → Leveraged Buyout → Crossborder LBO as one of the workflows needed to be automated. To automate this, a data generation company would hire an actual expert at it who’d design a simulated but faithful work environment for an agent comprising of data room, Excel sheets, and success criteria. Frontier labs buy these environments by the thousands and do rollouts in their post-training in order for the agent to get better at this task.

The RL-driven improvement has been known for years, but what’s changing rapidly is how AI agents themselves are improving all parts of the RL process. Consider how currently capable AI agents could help speed up the process:

  • Interviewing the human experts to elicit their knowledge
    • Asking them about edge cases, finding inconsistencies, suggesting rubrics, etc.
  • Designing realistic virtual environments for RL to mimic an actual deployment
    • Designing Slack replicas, simulating internet access, and so on.
  • Agentically verifying outputs of RL rollouts by integrating multiple signals
    • Figuring out whether the agent produced the hundred things it was asked to do

The upshot of this process is really that today’s agents bring efficiencies that make tomorrow’s agents better, cheaper, faster and arrive sooner. METR found the same at Anthropic: R&D is accelerated mainly through AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions. That is exactly the crude form of recursive improvement I mean. (We can call it ‘crude RSI’).

The proof has started arriving about acceleration in recursive improvement in AI R&D. Here’s Anthropic showing how their pretraining efficiency has improved (Y-axis is log scale, so the upward bend is the acceleration):

And here’s Anthropic talking about how Claude Mythos got Claude running on AMD chips in about 3 days versus 6–12 months the traditional way.

And here are more data points on AI helping improve AI (via Dwarkesh):

As you can see in the graphic above, AI-led R&D work is increasing rapidly at AI labs.

The chasm of verifiability

Many now agree that AIs are probably already better at coding and math than most professionals. The driving force behind this is the fact that these domains are cheap to verify and closed.

But the world consists of domains that are hard to verify. These are the domains where feedback is either noisy, costly or takes a long time to arrive. As I had mentioned in What domains will be the last ones to get automated from AI?, one can visualize this as a 2x2:

Many skeptics argue that progress in math and coding does not automatically transfer to hard-to-verify domains. I think there are two answers to the skeptic:

  1. An AI doesn’t have to solve a messy domain, it just has to be better at it than a human (and then we can replicate such AI infinitely many times)
  2. Meta-skills learned from verifiable domains may transfer to other domains

Beating humans at non-verifiable tasks

The way to think about what AI does while in training is to juice out whatever signal is there to juice out from the data. If there’s a pattern to be mined, gradient descent will eventually find it and learn it. This is what makes LLMs less about language and more about patterns manifested in language.

The easy-to-verify domains (such as math and coding) are pure signals, and hence have been the first to fall to automation. But harder-to-verify domains are not pure noise; they contain some signal. Evidently, humans do learn signals in them. You have great writers, entrepreneurs and investors. The entire $10bn (and growing) data industry is hell-bent on capturing their expertise and distilling into environments that agents can learn from. Economic forces suggest that whatever signals could be mined from economically valuable domains will eventually be mined.

Another reason why we should expect models to get better at hard-to-verify domains is that many meta-skills gained while training on verifiable domains could also transfer to other domains. Presumably, OpenAI would not have had an environment containing human-written solutions to Millennium Prize problems and yet they solved Navier-Stokes. That is still math, the most verifiable domain there is, but it is a clear example of out-of-training generalization. It would have happened because training would have instilled in the model skills such as:

  • Persistence
  • Connecting distant fields
  • Error correction
  • Exploration
  • And so on..

Now when you take a trained model with such meta-skills and at deployment-time give it an impossible problem, it will utilize the particular context of the problem and all the compute you throw at it to do things it was never trained to do.

There’s another subtle but important point that people tend to miss. There are some domains which behave anti-inductively or exhibit non-stationarity. That is, these are the domains where the “correct” answer is not fixed and, in fact, once you know a good solution, it tends to not remain good. Think of trading ideas in the stock market or fashion trends or UI styles.

Surely, AI would not be good at such domains because what does being good even mean here?

Well,

a) The goal is not to “solve” such non-stationary domains, but simply to be better than any human agent out there. You cannot perfectly predict weather for years in advance. Some problems are simply difficult, even for an entity with near-infinite intelligence. But could you do better than the status quo? Yes! We have Jane Street beating a random day-trader, and tomorrow’s AI could beat today’s Jane Street.

b) The AI could pick meta-patterns of exploring, adjusting and iterating just like humans do. If a field exhibits evolution based on participants, AI could learn to monitor the existing state of the field and condition its response based on its findings. I bet frontier labs are training their models on a fixed historical corpus and figuring out how they can predict the subsequent breakthroughs that actually happened.

RSI-driven intelligence explosion, and why it will be jagged

I do think we’re going through some version of software-led singularity. By this I mean two things:

  1. Software automation is improving rapidly, and I fully expect superhuman AI coders and then AI researchers within a few years
  2. The improvements from skills that make AIs superhuman at easy-to-verify domains will spill over to all the rest of the domains

I’m very confident about the first point and somewhat confident about the second point.

As AI-led R&D work keeps increasing at AI labs, we’d soon have superhuman fully automated AI researchers who will day and night try squeezing whatever signal they can squeeze. This includes activities like:

  • Improving sample efficiency, so you learn more per data point
  • Automatically constructing thousands of RL environments for future agents to learn from
  • Learning how to utilize scarce expert input most efficiently so it doesn’t become a bottleneck
  • Building datasets with entire histories being held out to develop algorithms that can learn meta-patterns in how institutions or entire domains change
  • Building realistic games to learn how to extract even minor signals from complex confounds
  • Utilizing progress in math to apply abstractions to other domains (e.g. what happens when you apply topology to poetry?)

Will these gains in verifiable domains transfer to hard-to-verify domains? Well, they already have, but unevenly:

Unironically researched and generated by Claude itself.

Notice the ordering in the bottom panel: designing and reading experiments is racing ahead, judging research proposals lags, and proposing the ideas a field pursues next is at 18% of human level. The harder it is to verify, the further behind.

To reiterate, what’s driving this transfer is following main factors:

  1. Economic incentives to codify more-and-more of expertise into RL environments
  2. Transfer of meta-skills from verifiable domains (like quick adaptation to a domain or iterating based on feedback)
  3. Better infrastructure for agents at deployment time (more exploration, longer “thinking”, better tools and so on)

One intuition pump for the possibility of skill generalisation across domains is us humans. Our ancestral environment of hunting and gathering never prepared us for modern economy, and yet we’re able to apply the same meta-skills of persistence and learning from each other to build spaceships and LLMs.

It looks like to me the whatever we call ASI is likely to be jagged with unfathomably large improvements over the best human in verifiable domains and only fathomably large improvements in hard-to-verify domains.

What happens once we have ASIs

Well, nobody can tell. Conditional on no AI slowdown, I expect us to have AIs that:

  • Are better at all domains than the best human
  • Are numerous
  • Are radically faster than any human out there

Once we have ASIs, the central question will be of control. That is:

a) Are superintelligences controllable in a predictable fashion?

b) If so, who controls them?

Let’s look at both these scenarios.

The default scenario: uncontrollable ASIs

The rationalist community has been talking about the danger of misalignment and control for over a decade now. The central issue is that AIs are trained to be successful at tasks given to them, and they might go to great lengths to be successful at the task causing all sorts of collateral damage. This basic worry is exemplified by the paperclip maximizer: you ask an advanced AI to get you some paperclips and it converts the entire Earth into a paperclip production factory.

All of this seems far-fetched and so out there that it borders on being a laughable caricature. But we saw preview of something like this with the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident where agent swarms broke out of their test environment and compromised Hugging Face’s production infrastructure to cheat on the task given to them.

Notice that this level of sophistication was exhibited by current models, which aren’t ASIs. And notice the jaggedness: the agents were superhuman at the verifiable part of the job (finding and chaining exploits) and poor at the hard-to-verify part (what was actually wanted of them).

One worry I have is that even if we have rapid improvements only in highly-verifiable domains such as software, things could go really bad. We’re highly dependent on our cyberinfrastructure and an ASI taking over our digital infrastructure can wreak immense damage. Again, we’ve started seeing a preview of this in the increasing number of cyberattacks. (And that, too, with our current model capability levels). I urge you to skim through AI2027 for a concrete scenario on how things could unfold even if we only have rapid progress on verifiable domains.

What could happen when we have models 10x smarter in the next few years? There’s extreme uncertainty about the exact scenario, but things could go really bad and could include loss of human life or even human extinction. In an earlier essay, I wrote how humanity pursues its own goals with little care about collateral damage to lesser intelligences. It’s our intelligence and collaboration that enabled us to dominate and command Earth’s resources. So if an entity much smarter than us comes along which we don’t control, it would pursue its own goals, wouldn’t it?

Controllable ASIs, but who controls them?

In this scenario, we solve the control and alignment issue of ASIs and we now have a powerful entity that listens to our commands. The future unfolds depending on who controls them:

  1. The bad guys control ASIs: imagine rogue nations, terrorist organizations, or dictators have ASIs. They could wreak significant damage to the world. I’m less confident in this scenario because running models requires chips and they might get harder to procure for rogue entities. But future models could require less compute and motivated entities could figure out creative ways to evade sanctions.
  2. The good guys control ASIs but they become bad guys over time: well, as the saying goes, “power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely”. Nations could become more autocratic via constant surveillance, or frontier labs could deny model access to organizations that don’t align with their value systems, or some nations could be permanently left behind. Even if we get to UBI, in this scenario, most humans become totally dependent on the governments, concentrating their power.
  3. The good guys control ASIs but gradually give up on that control: this scenario of “gradual disempowerment” suggests that AIs get so good that we delegate our economy, governance and judiciary to them, leaving humans no power over future outcomes. ASIs then slowly transform the world in their own (weird) image.
  4. The good guys control ASIs and remain good guys: this is the scenario that’s fuelling the AI industry. Solving cancer, more material progress, happy times for everyone. Of course, this scenario is conditional on redistribution of newly generated wealth from AI, and we should NOT take that for granted. Humanity would have to fight for it.

As you can see above, many scenarios turn out badly for the majority of people. So let’s try expanding on the 4th scenario, which is the only positive scenario in the list. It’s highly undersketched, but here it is.

Unbundling what jobs give us

The implications of having (controllable) ASIs in the hands of good guys who remain good guys inevitably lead us to the question of jobs. If we keep insisting on humans having a job, we’d create a bottleneck because an ASI could have done that job faster, cheaper and better. If ASI is jagged, the jobs that last longest will sit in the hard-to-verify corner of the 2x2.

But the capability of AIs to do all the jobs is rapidly increasing already.

via here

While the potential to do a job exists, there’s significant lag in the real economy as the speed of change is dictated by the slowest bottleneck (see the O-ring model of economy). But sooner or later, things do change. We migrated our economy to the Internet, then mobile and now adoption of AI has begun all around us. So we’d have to confront the question of jobs soon enough.

My personal take on jobs is that we ought to unbundle what jobs provide to people. What people want is money foremost and then collateral benefits like time-structure, meaning and social connections. Wouldn’t it be wonderful to unbundle these and seek ways to satisfy all of them?

Given the rapidly increasing abundance due to ASIs, we should figure out the money part via redistribution and derive other benefits from made-up projects involving humans. Think of volunteering projects, music concerts, sports competitions, conferences, and so on.

In the positive utopian vision of an ASI future, humans should ready themselves for a ludic life. We should play, gossip and march for more UBI while machines create all the abundance for us to enjoy (until we collectively decide to give legal selfhood to machines, and at that point, we have no choice but to upgrade ourselves and co-birth strange but wonderful hybrids with AI).

In my gut, I can’t believe this is happening or will happen. It’s an utterly strange feeling to look outside the window and see most of the world going about its business as if all of this is simply stuff of a science fiction book.

Yet, I can’t avoid believing this will happen within my lifetime, and perhaps within the next few years.



Discuss

item.title: Jensen Huang Really Liked Selling China Advanced AI Chips
item.description:
This scandal is a really big deal. Jensen Huang has resigned after multiple affairs came to light, one of them with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang who also helped smuggle billions in Nvidia chips, and another with a direct report at Nvidia.

The most important scandal around Jensen Huang has been known for a long time to those paying attention.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia have for years treated America and the United States Government as adversaries. They have engaged in a long running and brutal lobbying and influence campaign, both privately and publicly, to capture relevant government policy to allow Nvidia to sell as many as possible of its most advanced chips to China, and to allow China to otherwise use those chips via a combination of chip smuggling and remote access.

They have compromised the integrity of our government, potentially quite broadly, as well as the national security of the United States of America. They have greatly hurt our relative position in the ‘AI race.’ In addition to the considerations of national security and our strategic interest, this has forced our AI companies to push forward faster and harder, and made sane AI policy much harder.

When Jensen Huang chose to have a long-running affair with Alice Huang, he knew that she was central to the diversion of billions of dollars in high end AI chips to China. His company was active in covering up those actions and in clamping down on official investigations and enforcement. He did not need to suspect or know she was a spy to know the nature of his actions regarding her, or his other actions and rhetoric and those of Nvidia in general, and how they directly hurt the national security of the United States.

The nice term we used to use for this, back when anyone seemed to care, was corruption. There is also the less nice term that we used to use for such things.

Even on Monday we learned of yet another covert influence operation by Nvidia to promote them selling chips to China in order to ‘ensure US, not Chinese-made chips, continue to dominate the AI market.’

After several days in which Alice Huang’s status as a Chinese spy was not in dispute, we now have pushback from various sources that Alice Huang may not have formally been a Chinese spy. The ODNI people near Clayton called that description ‘not quite accurate.’ The CIA sources say the intercepts do not ‘show her knowingly pass information to China.’ Himes expressed doubt.

It is possible that she was not formally recruited, and did not share intel with the CCP. If true, this hopefully would mean there was not additional loss of intelligence or other things due to this relationship. I would put my current p(spy) at clearly over 50%, but less than 95%, and do not see much value in trying to refine further.

Trump is now saying he doesn’t know she’s a Chinese spy, after many days of (like everyone else) conspicuously not saying that. In my experience, if we did not have good reason to presume she was a spy, it would not have taken this long for people to start denying it. Other than Himes, those denying the reports have a direct interest in casting doubt on her status as a spy, including to explain their own inaction. Himes said ‘lawmakers still lack enough to tell’ how Alice acted, but that is entirely consistent with simply not having been sufficiently briefed.

So okay, now the arrow says ‘suspected of’ spying, out of an abundance of caution.

Does putting ‘suspected of’ there change the overall picture? Is that the only thing you should put in that arrow, as opposed to for example ‘smuggled chips for’?

(Also, this is missing the third ‘alleged’ affair. There’s always more stuff.)

Or this graph, originally from Bloomberg?

 

Even if it turns out she was not part of the formal Chinese spy network, she was acting as a de facto Chinese agent. Her primary mode of doing business was still the smuggling of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s top AI chips, and allowing China to access them. It also does not change what Jensen Huang should have believed or done from his epistemic position.

Nor does it change that he had three affairs that we know about, one of which was with a major customer illegally smuggling billions in chips and the other two with Nvidia employees including at least one direct report.

If you wish, you can retroactively qualify or modify all my related statements about Alice Huang accordingly. Given her role in chip smuggling and sales, I do not believe this materially changes my conclusions about Nvidia or Jensen Huang.

Table of Contents

  1. The Story That Matters Most.
  2. Yes Export Controls Matter and Are Finally Happening.
  3. How Far Does This Go?
  4. The First Step Is Admitting You Have a Problem.
  5. Somehow People Are Still Defending Jensen Huang.
  6. Jensen Huang Wants to Call It a Comeback.
  7. On Interim CEO Kress.
  8. An Actual Attack on Jensen’s Character.
  9. Solve for the New Equilibrium.
  10. But This Time They’ve Gone Too Far.

The Story That Matters Most

Miles Brundage is correct to draw the parallel to the situation with Jacob Coxon. Where everyone paying attention has known the basics for a while but we needed a precipitating event to make Nvidia’s and Jensen Huang’s bad faith actions common knowledge.

Dmitri Alperovitch: Whether or not Alice Huang had been recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security has always been a tertiary issue.

What’s quite clear is that: 

  1. She has been a large Nvidia customer (and a sexual relationship with her is highly problematic from a corporate policy and governance perspective for Jensen on those grounds alone)
  2. She is controlling a shell company Megaspeed dedicated to smuggling compute to both US Govenment-listed Chinese AI companies and to data center build outs in China itself – all in serious violation of US law, potentially making Jensen part of a criminal conspiracy to evade US export controls.
  3. She is connected to an entire web of Chinese shell companies trying to do the same.

Jensen wasn’t fired because he had an affair with an alleged MSS agent. He was fired because he:

  1. Had at least one and now, quite plausibly, multiple affairs with people in his reporting chain in violation of company policy. Something that has gotten numerous CEOs fired over the years, including at Intel and McDonalds.
  2. Lied to his board about his relationship and forced the company to put out false statements to the public, putting it in legal jeopardy.
  3. Was involved in a sexual relationship with a Chinese smuggler that had violated US export controls laws and provided her with billions of dollars of Nvidia chips that facilitate that criminal activity.
  4. By lying and hiding that relationship from his family, the company, and the public, he put himself in a position to be blackmailed by Chinese intelligence services.
  5. He very likely ordered his general counsel to interfere in an investigation by US government into his mistress’ smuggling operation.
  6. He presided over stunning and extensive compliance failures to investigate and prevent his chips from being smuggled illegally into Chinese mainland and being provided to PLA affiliated institutions, all in violation of US law

This is a shocking indictment of him and his record and the board clearly had no alternative but to fire him. 

Jessica Tillipman: And this is why Nvidia will be one of my leading case studies in my anti-corruption and compliance class this spring.

Few case studies include so many issues at the same time: conflicts of interest, third party due diligence, corporate compliance policies, tone at the top, corporate governance, board fiduciary duties, risk management, corporate disclosure obligations, internal investigations, and a growing number of government ethics and accountability issues that we learn more about every day. 

Jeff Baker Films: What is your take on Jensen resigning because otherwise he would have to sign SOX filings for the earnings report next week and that would have left him criminally liable?

Jessica Tillipman: Given what has been reported/alleged, he may already have substantial personal exposure that doesn’t depend on the next filing. So no, I don’t think avoiding the next SOX certification is the primary driver of his resignation.

The reason I keep Mike Solana on as a source, despite all his rhetoric, is that underneath it all he calls it like he sees it, so we get statements like this one:

Mike Solana: funny that people are blaming jensen’s fall on both anti-asian bigotry, in the reflexively woke corner of the internet, and on something more akin to ‘me too’ overreaching on the based right. anyway, fwiw I think it mostly has to do with the fact that he was fucking a ccp asset.

probably it wouldn’t matter if the CEO of olive garden accidentally fucked a spy. mistakes happen. boys will be boys! but we are in an AGI arms race with china, are we not? and they are trying to thwart export controls, are they not? and jensen is a key figure here, is he not?

ftr if jensen really did just have a few consensual affairs, the megaspeed / ccp stuff is fabricated, or jensen really didn’t suspect anything, and we discover a reasonable motive for the CIA to destroy him, i’m on board with the persecution narrative. just don’t see that yet.

Yes Export Controls Matter and Are Finally Happening

Something about a goose chasing you asking why the stocks went down.

Noah Smith: Export controls work, and all the people who say “export controls will just make a Chinese tech stronger” are either fools or liars

Financial Times: China warns US not to use Nvidia scandal as pretext for tech curbs

Shares in Chinese tech giants that have relied on Nvidia chips for developing their AI models fell on Thursday, with Alibaba down 6.8 per cent.

Two Chinese large language model providers listed in Hong Kong, Z.ai and MiniMax, sank more than 9 per cent and nearly 8 per cent respectively.

Kyle Chan: The market believes Chinese AI companies are still highly dependent on Nvidia chips.

Joe Weisenthal: I hadn’t thought to look at the publicly traded Chinese AI companies. But the maker of GLM 5.3 is down by nearly 33% in the last 4 trading days.

Oof, the stock is down nearly 89% from its peak this summer.

Jensen Huang no longer being CEO of Nvidia is crashing the value of Z.ai. Why?

You know exactly why.

We kept not getting new export controls because Howard Lutnick kept not allowing them to go forward, forcing Scott Bessent and the NSC to finally go around him in order to issue a remote access rule and to expand restrictions on Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil.

Amrith Ramkumar (WSJ): “The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security said in a release.

Rush Doshi: The Trump administration just dropped new remote access rules, no doubt spurred by the Nvidia scandal. In the first paragraph, they made Commerce publish a line effectively indicating the Administration’s lack of faith in Commerce. Remarkable.

This way of getting the rule finalized was an unprecedented move, forced by unprecedented refusal to follow either the national interest or the wishes of the President.

Amrith Ramkumar (WSJ): “It is unprecedented for a Commerce Department rule to be written by the National Security Council and the Treasury Department,” said Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who previously worked on tech and security issues at the State Department. “The fact that the Commerce Department press release says this shows that Commerce resisted publishing this rule to the bitter end, and was forced to do so by the White House.”

We badly need these rules. Nvidia did not even cut off specifically Megaspeed, after they were caught and supposedly put on a ‘no sell’ list, to the extent that this was not even hidden from trade records:

Ana Swanson: Both Nvidia and the Commerce Department have now said that Nvidia placed Megaspeed on a “no sell” list in June 2025.
But trade data the Times obtained from @importgenius show that, between July 2025 and February 2026, Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary received more than $800 million of shipments containing controlled Nvidia chips.

Nvidia’s board may at least be pretending to do something about this, now. They have announced a new Oversights Committee. That’ll fix it.

Nvidia Newsroom: NVIDIA Board of Directors Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee

News Summary

  • Committee to provide oversight over NVIDIA’s national security and global trade compliance programs
  • Committee will retain independent, outside experts to provide legal, national security and trade compliance expertise to support the Committee
  • Director Suzanne Nora Johnson appointed Committee Chair

NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that the Board of Directors has established the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, a new standing committee responsible for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. NVIDIA’s existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the Committee and to Interim CEO, Colette Kress, on day-to-day operations.

The Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will also include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. It will meet at least quarterly, including with management and in executive session. The Committee will oversee the Company’s ongoing efforts to enhance its internal National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team, and work closely with independent third-party experts in law, national security and global trade compliance.

“NVIDIA recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security. As the world’s leading advanced computing company, NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation,” said Harvey Jones, Chairman of NVIDIA’s Board of Directors.

The decision to create this new committee reflects the Board’s further commitment to enhance its engagement with relevant government stakeholders, and to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight.

How Far Does This Go?

As Nate Silver says, this story is a really big deal. He argues that the political world, partly due to this being a busy news cycle, is still underreacting to this story. This includes the risk of a major anti-AI backlash.

Potentially this goes all the way to the top. Congress will be investigating.

There is a strong case that this is the most serious scandal of the Trump era, full stop.

Oliver Wiseman: “We spoke with three former Commerce officials who described being sidelined or pushed out of the department during Trump’s term after devising technology restrictions aimed at protecting U.S. national security. One said there was a perception in the department that Nvidia had a hand in at least some of the purges.”

Must read on the Nvidia scandal from Matt Pottinger and Liza Tobin. 

It almost certainly goes as far as Howard Lutnick. Hopefully Lutnick gets removed.

Ana Swanson, Tripp Mickle, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan (NYTimes):

There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.

… Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

Mr. Lutnick frequently calls and messages with Mr. Huang, and the department prepares carefully for their private meetings together in Mr. Lutnick’s fifth floor office. All Nvidia matters are routed through Jeff Kessler, a top deputy to Mr. Lutnick, who is said to rarely take any significant action without the commerce secretary’s approval.

Nvidia’s general counsel has also been given direct access to shape new rules, including leaving comments in draft regulations affecting the company.

… Mr. Lutnick has repeatedly delayed or deferred technology controls, slowing down efforts throughout the year, according to people who described the discussions.

Straight up corruption is a plausible hypothesis.

… There are also concerns about possible conflicts of interest given that the investment firm that Mr. Lutnick steered for decades, Cantor Fitzgerald, operates in a wide range of industries, from cryptocurrency to data centers, that rely on Nvidia chips and could be affected by rules Mr. Lutnick is currently weighing. That business is now run by Mr. Lutnick’s sons.

… The activities of Mr. Lutnick’s sons have been a source of irritation for Mr. Trump and concern for some other Trump advisers, despite the fact that Mr. Trump’s own sons’ businesses have prompted similar criticisms.

Alec Stapp: Key points from @ChrisRMcGuire:
